message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold a maximum of **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a month‑to‑month tenancy).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control). | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or letter) of any needed repairs.
• If repairs are not made within a reasonable time, you may withhold rent or repair and deduct (see below). | | **Repair & Deduct / Rent Withholding** | • If the landlord fails to fix a major problem, you may:
 1. **Repair and deduct** from your rent (up to the amount of the repair).
 2. **Withhold rent** until the issue is fixed.
 3. **Terminate the lease** if the problem is severe and unaddressed. | • Keep receipts and document the issue.
• Provide written notice to the landlord before withholding or repairing. | | **Privacy & Entry** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of all entries. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Lease Terms** | • The lease must be in writing if it lasts longer than one year.
• The lease can’t contain illegal clauses (e.g., waiving your right to a habitable unit). | • Review the lease carefully before signing. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the **Texas Property Code** eviction procedures: written notice, filing a lawsuit, and obtaining a court order.
• Common grounds: non‑payment of rent, lease violations, or the landlord’s own need for the property. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• Seek legal counsel if you receive an eviction notice. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has **no statewide rent‑control laws**. | • Rent increases must be in accordance with the lease or a new lease agreement. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities before moving in. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • You may sublet or assign the lease only with the landlord’s written consent (unless the lease prohibits it). | • Obtain written permission and keep a copy. | | **Insurance** | • Landlords are not required to provide renter’s insurance, but you’re encouraged to obtain it. | • Keep proof of insurance if requested. | | **Legal Assistance** | • Texas offers free or low‑cost legal aid for tenants (e.g., Texas Legal Services Center, local bar associations). | • Contact a local tenant advocacy group or legal aid office. | #### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the lease in full.** Look for clauses about repairs, deposits, entry, and termination. 2. **Ask for a move‑in inspection report.** Document existing conditions. 3. **Confirm who pays utilities.** 4. **Verify the landlord’s right to enter.** 5. **Check for any prohibited clauses** (e.g., waiving your right to a habitable unit). 6. **Keep copies of all communications** (emails, letters, texts). #### When Things Go Wrong - **Notice in Writing:** Always give the landlord written notice of any problem. - **Document Everything:** Photos, videos, receipts, and a written log of communications. - **Seek Mediation:** Many cities offer mediation services for landlord‑tenant disputes. - **File a Complaint:** If discrimination or illegal eviction occurs, file with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or HUD. - **Legal Counsel:** If the landlord threatens eviction or refuses to make repairs, consult a lawyer or tenant advocacy group. --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, a fair security deposit process, privacy, and protection against discrimination. If a landlord violates these rights, you have several remedies—repair and deduct, rent withholding, lease termination, or legal action. Keep thorough records and seek professional help if needed.
